explanations.answer: How long will the wicked exult
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 3 says, "How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?" He says it twice in a row. I think a question that comes out twice has been sitting on him a while. And notice he takes it straight to the LORD.

explanations.answer: Why have You hidden Your face
explanations.explanation: That's a question people do bring to God, but it isn't the one in verse 3. Here the writer asks, "How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?" He repeats "How long will the wicked…" and it's about the wicked celebrating. Good news is you can still pick the right one from the case, friend.

explanations.answer: Who can stand before Your anger
explanations.explanation: Nope, that line isn't in this psalm. In verse 3 he asks, "How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?" He's looking at the wicked cheering, and he wants to know how long it lasts. He asks it two times, like a man who really wants an answer.
That's it. Verse 5 says, "They crush Your people, O LORD; they oppress Your heritage." The writer is telling the LORD about the people who belong to Him. He says it straight to Him, no sugarcoating.
Not enemies, friend. Verse 5 says the wicked crush the LORD's people and oppress His heritage. The ones getting crushed are the ones who belong to Him. I think this one hurts.
Idols don't show up anywhere in this verse. The writer says, "They crush Your people, O LORD…" It's people getting crushed, and he tells the LORD about it plainly. I think this one hurts.

True. In verse 7 the wicked say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed." That's their whole theory, and the writer is about to answer it. It's a theory with no homework behind it, friend.

Close, but the psalm does say it. In verse 7 the wicked say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed." Those are their words, quoted right there in the psalm. Hang on for verse 9, where the writer asks about the ear and the eye.
Yes, ear. Verse 9 says, "He who affixed the ear, can He not hear?" It's the first half of the writer's comeback. The One who put the ear on the head surely hears. Pretty hard to argue with that one.
Yes, eye. Verse 9 goes on, "He who formed the eye, can He not see?" In verse 7 the wicked said, "The LORD does not see…" Here the writer asks whether the One who formed the eye does not see.

Hand isn't in this verse, friend. The writer talks about the ear and the eye. He asks if the One who affixed the ear cannot hear, and if the One who formed the eye cannot see. If he'd gone with hands, my mustache and I would have had some thoughts.

The mouth doesn't come up in verse 9. The question is about hearing and seeing, so it's the ear and the eye. The wicked had plenty to say with their mouths in verse 4, but that's not what he's answering here.

Heart is a good guess, but verse 9 doesn't use it. He says, "He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see?" The ear and the eye answer the wicked saying the LORD does not see and pays no heed.

Not this time, friend. Verse 10 asks, "He who teaches man, does He lack knowledge?" It's a question, and the writer asks it because he's sure the answer is no. The One who teaches man isn't short on knowledge.

False is right. Verse 10 asks, "He who admonishes the nations, does He not discipline? He who teaches man, does He lack knowledge?" It's a question, not a statement that the LORD lacks knowledge. The writer asks it about the One who teaches man.
Futile is right. Verse 11 says, "The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile." The LORD knows them all, even the 2 a.m. ones that go nowhere. I've had a few plans like that myself.
Hidden isn't the word. Verse 11 says the LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile. The writer calls the thoughts futile, not hidden. Futile is the word to look for, friend.

Pure would be nice, but that's not what the verse says. The writer says, "The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile." He's talking to the fools, so he's not handing out compliments here.

explanations.answer: The man the LORD disciplines and teaches
explanations.explanation: That's him. Verse 12 says, "Blessed is the man You discipline, O LORD, and teach from Your law…" The writer calls the man blessed who is disciplined and taught. I bet discipline isn't the first thing most of us would put on a blessing list. Disciplined and taught, and still called blessed.

explanations.answer: The man who never faces any trouble
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Verse 13 talks about relief from days of trouble, so trouble is in the picture. The one called blessed in verse 12 is the man the LORD disciplines and teaches from His law.

explanations.answer: The man who pays the wicked back
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't say that. In verse 12 the blessed one is the man the LORD disciplines and teaches from His law. Payback shows up later, and it's the LORD who brings it in verse 23.

explanations.answer: To grant him relief from days of trouble
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verses 12 and 13 read, "Blessed is the man You discipline, O LORD, and teach from Your law, to grant him relief from days of trouble" The trouble is still named in the verse, and so is the relief. Discipline and teaching on one side, relief on the other, all in one sentence.

explanations.answer: To make him rich in the land
explanations.explanation: Money never comes up in these verses, friend. The text says the LORD teaches him from His law "…to grant him relief from days of trouble…" That's the purpose the writer gives.

explanations.answer: To set him over the nations
explanations.explanation: Nothing about ruling over nations here. Verse 13 says it's "…to grant him relief from days of trouble…" The writer names that one purpose, so I'll stick with it.

Forsake, yes. Verse 14 says, "For the LORD will not forsake His people; He will never abandon His heritage." The wicked crush them, and the writer still says that. I know a little about sitting in the dark of a junk drawer for years, so that line lands with me.
Not judge, friend. Verse 14 says, "For the LORD will not forsake His people…" Forsake is the word the writer picks. Then he says it again in different words: He will never abandon His heritage.
Rebuke isn't in this verse. The writer says, "For the LORD will not forsake His people; He will never abandon His heritage." He says it twice in different words, which tells you he means it.

Righteous is right. Verse 15 says, "Surely judgment will again be righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it." He says it after listing everything the wicked did. That's some steady faith, friend.

Delayed makes sense, since he did ask "how long" back in verse 3. But in verse 15 he says, "Surely judgment will again be righteous…" The word is righteous, and he says the upright in heart will follow it.
Silent is close to a word from verse 17, but not this verse. Verse 15 says, "Surely judgment will again be righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it." Righteous is the one.

Close, but one little word flips it. Verse 17 says, "Unless the LORD had been my helper, I would soon have dwelt in the abode of silence." The writer didn't end up there, because the LORD was his helper. That "unless" is doing a lot of work.

False is right. Verse 17 says, "Unless the LORD had been my helper, I would soon have dwelt in the abode of silence." That's what would have happened without the LORD's help. He says the LORD was his helper.

Supports, yes. In verse 18 the writer says that if he says his foot is slipping, then "Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me." Picture slipping on a floor covered in flour. That loving devotion is what holds him up.

Tests isn't the word. In verse 18 the writer says that if he says his foot is slipping, then "Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me." Supports is the word he uses. The LORD's loving devotion is the one doing it.

Leaves doesn't fit, friend. In verse 18 the writer says that if he says his foot is slipping, then "Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me." Supports is the word he uses. The LORD's loving devotion is the one doing it.
That's it, friend. Verse 19 says, "When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul." The writer doesn't hide the anxiety. He names it, and then he names what delights his soul anyway.
Vengeance is how the psalm starts, in verse 1. But in verse 19 he says, "When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul." When he's anxious, it's consolation that delights him.
Commands aren't named in this verse, friend. The writer says, "When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul." It's the consolation that does the delighting.
Yes. Verse 22 says, "But the LORD has been my stronghold, and my God is my rock of refuge." The wicked are ganging up, and the writer says that. A stronghold and a rock don't wobble.
Those are lovely words, but they're not what verse 22 says. It reads, "But the LORD has been my stronghold, and my God is my rock of refuge." Think of a place that keeps him safe when people gang up.

Nice pair, friend, but not this verse. Verse 22 says, "But the LORD has been my stronghold, and my God is my rock of refuge." That's the picture the writer paints right after the wicked band together.

True. Verse 23 says, "He will bring upon them their own iniquity and destroy them for their wickedness." The writer says it plainly, and he says it with confidence. The verse ends, "The LORD our God will destroy them."

The psalm does say it, friend. Verse 23 reads, "He will bring upon them their own iniquity and destroy them for their wickedness." It's what the writer says the LORD will do, and it's how the psalm ends.
